declarations.name: createHelixCemConfig
declarations.description:
Builds the analyzer config for a Helix package.

Every package that ships custom elements uses this rather than configuring
the analyzer itself, so that a new plugin is added once here instead of
being copied into each package and drifting.

declarations.default: 'HelixElement'

declarations.name: isCustomElement
declarations.description: True only for declarations that register themselves as a custom element.

declarations.name: classIndex
declarations.description: Indexes every class declaration by name across a set of manifests.

declarations.name: descendsFrom
declarations.description:
True when a declaration is `root` or descends from it.

Walks the `superclass` chain, which crosses package boundaries as long as the
dependency's manifest is in the index. Terminates on cycles, which a
hand-edited manifest could contain.

declarations.name: eachComponent
declarations.default: function* ( manifest: HelixManifest, context?: HelixContext, ): Generator<{ declaration: HelixDeclaration; module: HelixModule }> { const index = classIndex([manifest, ...(context?.thirdPartyCEMs ?? [])]) for (const module of manifest.modules ?? []) { for (const declaration of module.declarations ?? []) { if (declaration.kind === 'class' && descendsFrom(declaration, index)) { yield { declaration, module } } } } }
declarations.description:
Every Helix component in a manifest, paired with its module.

A component is any class descending from `HelixElement`, registered or not.
That covers the headless tier, which carries no `@customElement` decorator,
while excluding utility classes and the `declare class` interfaces that back
mixins. Keying on "is a class" instead would lint and stamp every exported
class in the package, which is correct only until someone exports one that is
not a component.

Pass `context` so the superclass chain can be resolved across packages;
without it, a component whose base lives in a dependency looks unrelated to
`HelixElement` and is skipped.

declarations.name: createSheet
declarations.description:
Builds a stylesheet from CSS authored in a `.css` file.

Component styles live in real `.css` files rather than `css` tagged
templates, so they get CSS tooling: syntax highlighting, formatters, the
token linter, and a diff that reads as CSS. `bun run styles` compiles each
one into a sibling `.css.ts` that calls this.

The `unsafe` in `unsafeCSS` warns about interpolating untrusted input into a
stylesheet. That is not what happens here: the argument is a build-time
constant read from a file in this repo, never a runtime value. Wrapping it
keeps the warning where it belongs, on `unsafeCSS` itself, and gives one seam
to change if constructable stylesheets become the better primitive.

Base class for every Helix element.

Owns only what is universal: shadow-root normalization and the shared
lifecycle surface. Anything visual belongs in the styled tier; anything
component-specific belongs in the component.
declarations.name: HelixElement

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: emit
members.description:
Dispatches a composed, bubbling CustomEvent. Kebab-case names map to React
`onFooBar` props through the wrapper generator, so event names are part of
the public API and should be treated as such.

declarations.name: createComponent
declarations.description:
Wraps a custom element as a React component.

Two things React does not do for custom elements, and this does:

**Custom events.** React only knows how to bind its own synthetic event
names. `open-change` is not one, so `onOpenChange` is attached with
`addEventListener` directly and the detail is passed through, which is what
makes the callback receive `{ open: true }` rather than a raw Event.

**Non-attribute properties.** Attributes stringify. An object or array
crossing the boundary as an attribute arrives as `[object Object]`, so
anything in `properties` is assigned to the element instead. Booleans go the
same route so `false` removes rather than setting `"false"`, which is truthy
as an attribute.

declarations.name: deriveTheme
declarations.description:
Computes a complete token set from intent inputs.

Foreground colors are solved for their contrast target rather than picked and
then audited, so a passing theme is guaranteed by construction. Anything that
could not reach its target at the requested chroma is reported in
`violations` rather than silently shipped.

declarations.name: toCss
declarations.description: Renders a derived theme as a CSS custom-property block.

declarations.name: oklchToLinearRgb
declarations.description:
OKLCH to linear sRGB, via OKLab. Coefficients from Björn Ottosson's
definition of the Oklab color space.

declarations.name: isOutOfGamut
declarations.description: True when the color falls outside the sRGB gamut and would be clipped.

declarations.name: oklchToHex
declarations.description: OKLCH to a `#rrggbb` string, clipped into gamut.

declarations.name: relativeLuminance
declarations.description:
WCAG 2.1 relative luminance. Computed from linear-light values, which we
already have, so no round trip through gamma-encoded sRGB is needed.

declarations.name: contrastRatio
declarations.description: WCAG contrast ratio between two colors, from 1 to 21.

declarations.name: fitToGamut
declarations.description:
Reduces chroma until the color falls inside the sRGB gamut, preserving
lightness and hue.

Without this, any seed chroma at an extreme lightness silently produces a
clipped color: a near-white surface with a hint of brand tint pushes a
channel above 1.0 and gets truncated on the way to hex, which breaks both the
intended hue and the contrast that was solved for.

declarations.name: lightnessForContrast
declarations.description:
Finds the lightness at which `sample` hits `target` contrast against
`background`.

This is the function the whole theming product rests on. It is what lets a
user pick a brand color and receive a palette whose every foreground and
background pair is accessible **by construction**, rather than generated and
then audited.

**Both directions are tried unless one is pinned.** Whether light or dark
text works better on a given surface is not knowable from the background's
luminance alone: a mid-tone brand color often fails white text and passes
black, and a luminance-threshold heuristic picks wrong exactly there. When
both sides pass, the least extreme result wins.

Returns the closest achievable lightness when the target is unreachable at
the sample's chroma, so callers should verify with `contrastRatio` rather
than assume success.

declarations.name: composition
declarations.description:
Derives a component's composition group and part from its module path.

Each part owns a folder, so the two directory levels above the file are the
group and the part:

  src/card/root/card-root.ts       -> Card.Root
  src/card/header/card-header.ts   -> Card.Header
  src/scroll-area/root/…           -> ScrollArea.Root

Deriving this from the tag name instead is ambiguous in exactly the cases
that matter: `helix-scroll-area` is one component, `helix-card-header` is
part of another, and nothing in either name distinguishes them. Folders
already encode the author's intent, so they are the honest source.

Recording it in the manifest rather than recomputing it in each generator
means the React wrappers, the docs site, and anything else agree on what
belongs together, and a regrouping shows up as a manifest diff.

declarations.name: conventionLint
declarations.description:
Enforces the documented Helix conventions against the manifest.

These rules are written down in `CLAUDE.md`, which means they are followed
exactly as often as someone remembers them. Checking them here turns prose
into a gate, and does it at the layer where the consequences actually land:
the manifest is what IDE tooltips, wrapper generators, and code-authoring
agents read, so an undocumented property is invisible tooling-wide, not just
untidy.

declarations.name: declaredEvents
declarations.description:
Drops events the analyzer inferred rather than ones we declared.

The analyzer records an event for every `dispatchEvent` call it can see. When
the call sits inside a generic helper, the name it records is the *parameter
identifier*, not an event name: `HelixElement.emit(name, detail)` yields a
phantom event called `name` on every element that inherits it.

Helix requires every event to be declared with `@event` on the component that
exposes it, precisely because a dispatch inside a mixin or a base helper is
not something the analyzer can name correctly. Anything without a description
therefore came from inference, not from us.

Runs before the convention linter so the linter validates declared events
only, and an `@event` tag with an empty description still fails.

declarations.name: helixTier
declarations.description:
Stamps every Helix component with the design-system tier it belongs to.

Downstream consumers need this and cannot infer it: the React wrapper
generator wraps only the styled tier (wrapping headless would ship unstyled
components under the same names), and the docs site labels the two
differently. Recording it in the manifest keeps that knowledge in one place
rather than duplicated as a path heuristic in every generator.

declarations.name: toReactProp
declarations.description:
Converts a kebab-case event name to its React prop.

`open-change` becomes `onOpenChange`, matching what
`@wc-toolkit/react-wrappers` generates.

declarations.name: reactEvents
declarations.description:
Records the React prop name generated for each event.

The mapping is a convention (kebab event to `onFooBar` prop) that is
currently implicit in the wrapper generator. Writing it into the manifest
makes it inspectable: an agent reading the manifest learns the React API
without knowing the generator's rules, and a drift between the documented
event and the shipped prop becomes visible in a diff.

Grafts controlled and uncontrolled open state onto a base class.

Controlled mode is detected automatically: once a consumer sets `open`
explicitly, the element stops managing the value itself and only emits
`open-change`. Uncontrolled consumers set `defaultOpen` and let the element
own it.

The kebab-case `open-change` event maps to an `onOpenChange` React prop
through the wrapper generator, so the event name is public API.

Sets `data-open` on the host whenever the element is open, in either mode.
Styled tiers should select on that rather than on `[open]`, which is absent
for uncontrolled consumers.
declarations.name: WithOpen

members.name: isOpen
members.description: The resolved open state, whichever mode the element is in.

members.name: reflectResolvedState
members.description:
Mirrors the resolved state onto the host as `data-open`.

`open` only reflects in controlled mode, so styling on `:host([open])`
silently does nothing for uncontrolled consumers. Presentation needs one
selector that is true whenever the element is actually open, in either
mode.

members.name: setOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change. In uncontrolled mode the element updates
itself; in controlled mode it only notifies and waits for the consumer.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open. Setting this puts the element into
controlled mode: the consumer owns the value from that point on.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `open` is set.

declarations.default: class HelixBaseCard extends HelixElement { constructor() { super(...arguments); /** Cached so a re-render does not clear a name that has not changed. */ this.labelledBy = null; this.handleSlotChange = () => { this.adoptTitle(); }; } connectedCallback() { super.connectedCallback(); this.adoptTitle(); } /** * Points the region at the first descendant title, if there is one. * * Searches the light DOM rather than the shadow root: the title is the * consumer's child, not ours. `querySelector` reaches nested titles, so a * title inside a header still names the card. */ adoptTitle() { const title = this.querySelector('helix-card-title, helix-base-card-title'); // `||` rather than `??`: an element with no id has `id === ''`, which is // not nullish, so `??` would accept it and emit `aria-labelledby=""`. An // empty reference is worse than no reference, because it names the group // as the empty string rather than leaving it unnamed. const id = title?.id || null; if (id !== this.labelledBy) { this.labelledBy = id; this.requestUpdate(); } } /** * Adopts again once the first render has happened. * * `connectedCallback` runs before a parser-created element's children exist, * so the first pass finds nothing. `slotchange` is supposed to cover that and * does in browsers, but it only fires on *initial* assignment in some * implementations, so a card that depends solely on it renders unnamed under * a DOM that does not. Both hooks, and `adoptTitle` is idempotent. */ firstUpdated(changed) { super.firstUpdated(changed); this.adoptTitle(); } render() { return html ` <section id=${REGION_ID} aria-labelledby=${ifDefined(this.labelledBy ?? undefined)} part="container" role="group" > <slot @slotchange=${this.handleSlotChange}></slot> </section> `; } }
declarations.description:
Cards group related content and actions into a single surface.

The root owns the surface and the accessible name. Its parts are separate
elements rather than slots on one element, because a card's regions are
independently styleable, independently omittable, and frequently reordered:
`Card.Header`, `Card.Title`, `Card.Body`, `Card.Footer`.

**Naming is coordinated, not assumed.** A card that groups content needs an
accessible name or it is an unlabelled group, which screen readers announce
as noise. Rather than requiring every consumer to pass `aria-label`, the root
looks for a `helix-card-title` in its light DOM and points at it. That
coordination is the whole reason these are compound components: a title
nested three levels down still names the card that contains it.

Titles name the card that contains them.

The element ensures it has an id, because `Card.Root` names itself by
pointing `aria-labelledby` at this title and cannot point at an element with
no id. Consumers may set their own id and it is left alone.

declarations.description:
Disclosures let users show and hide a section of related content.

The headless tier owns structure, accessibility wiring, and state. It ships
no CSS and references no tokens: styling is the styled tier's job. Consumers
who want to bring their own styling entirely can use this tier directly.

`open`, `defaultOpen`, `isOpen`, and `setOpen` come from the `WithOpen` mixin
and resolve into this component's manifest automatically, because
`@helix-io/core` publishes one and the analyzer runs with
`dependencies: true`.

Content stays mounted when closed and is hidden by the styled tier's CSS.
Unmounting it made an open/close transition impossible, and `hidden` is
`display: none`, which cannot transition either. `inert` keeps closed content
out of the tab order and the accessibility tree without removing it from the
box tree.

The event is declared here rather than inferred. It is dispatched through a
generic helper, and the analyzer can only record the parameter identifier of
a dynamic dispatch, not the name it resolves to at runtime.

Bodies hold a card's main content.

A separate element rather than a slot on the root, so it can be styled,
omitted, and reordered independently.

members.description:

silently does nothing for uncontrolled consumers. Presentation needs one
selector that is true whenever the element is actually open, in either

itself; in controlled mode it only notifies and waits for the consumer.
